## Introduction

Research on the early and sustained success of turnaround schools and districts repeatedly

emphasizes the significance of strong leadership (Dodman, 2014; Hill 2016; Hitt & Tucker,

2015; Hitt & Meyers, 2018). Research on the topic covers a variety of topics including leader

identity, training, mindsets, beliefs, and actions. This paper investigates how principals and other

school leaders in a southern school district, here called the “Transform Schools” navigate the

demands of turnaround reform while engaging with facets of culturally responsive leadership.

Transform School leaders are expected to make rapid academic growth within the lowest-

performing schools in the state. They must also consider the unique demands of their schools’

individual contexts including the sociohistorical positioning of local neighborhoods.

Accounting for this convergence of factors, this paper analyzes how leader considerations

of school communities’ culture and identity inform their approach to turnaround leadership. The

Transform Schools neighborhoods appear similar to many other turnaround districts across the

country, characterized by high-poverty, majority minority student populations experiencing and

responding to years of academic underachievement. Yet, to summarize the Transform Schools,

its city, or any of its segmented neighborhoods as a collection of demographic variables fails to

account for the nuance of how place and culture influence the work of school leaders. Transform

leaders’ ability to perform the extreme task of school turnaround was in part dependent on their

ability to competently engage with these neighborhood identities. This paper engages research on

turnaround leadership and culturally relevant leadership to investigate how school leaders in a

southern, urban school district applied considerations of school communities’ culture and

identity to turnaround leadership practice.

Turnaround Leadership Frameworks

Research has established school leaders as crucial factors in student achievement (Day et al.,

2009; Leithwood, Patten, and Jantzi, 2010). For chronically underachieving schools, leadership

can take on increased significance (Murphy & Meyers, 2008). There is a substantial body of

literature exploring the nuances and crucial elements that make for an effective school leader.

Effective leadership and turnaround leadership have overlap but there are qualities that are

specific and unique to the role of a turnaround leader (Meyers & Hitt, 2017). Although

turnaround leaders do in fact embody elements of effective leadership, the unique circumstances

of their positions demand additional skills and competencies. “Turnaround” as operationalized

here is adapted from Meyers & Hitt (2018), as a context where districts are tasked with creating

rapid annual academic gains in core tested subjects (e.g., math or English Language Arts) for the

bottom five percent of schools, while operating under threat of state takeover or school closure.

Although sustained improvement is often a long-term goal of turnaround efforts, that is not

necessarily embedded in this conceptualization of turnaround.

Turnaround leaders are here defined as principals, assistant principals, and other school- or

district-level personnel operating in a turnaround context. Due to the high-stake pressures and

significance challenges and deficits these leaders are often responsible for tackling, their roles

differ from those of leaders in other contexts. For example, a review of school turnaround

principal identified a dozen areas in which principals must be adept and a dozen more necessary

traits (Meyers & Hitt, 2017). Although these turnaround principals fulfilled the expectations

established by theories around effective school leadership, there was an additional incompletely

articulated quality which differentiated these leaders from their peers outside of turnaround

contexts.

While the exact nature of this quality remains elusive, the authors concluded that turnaround

leaders do “see, feel and think differently” (Meyers & Hitt, 2017, p.53). A recent proposed

framework for “sustained turnaround leadership” delineates 43 practices identified from

literature devoted to understanding successful turnaround practice (Hitt & Meyers, 2018). These

practices are categorized into five domains relating to a vision for schooling, mobilizing teachers

in organizational transformation, instructional leadership, high academic expectations, and

working with partners outside the school. Such frameworks are crucial to understanding how to

create and support effective turnaround practice. However, there remains space to further refine

and explore how other effective leadership practices can influence turnaround work.

Culturally Responsive Leadership

Culturally relevant leadership is here applied as a quality that may influence the construction of

turnaround leadership competencies. Culturally relevant pedagogy (CRP) as perhaps most

recognizably conceptualized by Gloria Ladson-Billings (1995) is defined by “an ability to

develop students academically, a willingness to nurture and support cultural competence, and the

development of a sociopolitical or critical consciousness” (p. 482). Since then, numerous

scholars have expanded upon this concept, further delineating its meaning and varied application

in the classroom (Gay, 2010). Across these definitions is a shared goal of fostering educational

practice that considers how the holistic teaching and learning experience, include the

environment, norms, expectations, and activities engage and affirm the cultural positioning of

students (Lomotey & Lowery, 2016; Gay, 2010; Ladson-Billings, 1995).

Although CRP is most frequently applied to classroom teaching, the past two decades have

seen increasing attention to how school leaders can employ or foster culturally responsive

education within and beyond the classroom. For example, a recent review of literature

concerning culturally responsive leadership was conducted by Khalifa and colleagues (2018).

They identified culturally responsive leadership behaviors that included a “critical self-

awareness,” where leaders are constantly engaging with how their identities and value systems

influence their work and impact the communities they are there to serve. Culturally responsive

leaders also cultivate schools that embody these practices through instructional and leadership

staff development, curriculum adoption, and school climate. Additionally, these leaders are

actively engaging and responding to families, students, and other community actors in the

process of education.

Research Context

The Transform Schools are a collection schools in a large urban school district located in the

Southern United States. These schools were identified as among the lowest-achieving in the state

based upon state assessment scores. As a result, a plan was put in place to orchestrate the

“turnaround” of the district. The three possible turnaround strategies taken are allocation to the

Transform Schools, takeover by a charter management organization, or closure. Although both

the charter schools and the Transform Schools were overseen by district staff, only the

Transform Schools were operated solely by the district. Schools that failed to meet growth

metrics were under threat of takeover by a charter management organization or closure.

Central to the Transform School original strategy was the placement of top-performing

district leaders into its highest-need schools. As a result, the participants of this study all had

reputations and track records of producing positive growth in low-achieving schools either in the

district or the state. Like many other turnaround leaders, those of the Transform Schools were

expected to produce rapid and significant results. In the first few years, TRANSFORM leaders


<!-- Page 6 -->


DRAFT – PLEASE DO NOT DUPLICATE / CIRCULATE

5

were granted near complete autonomy around school management including curriculum,

disciplinary policies, and teacher hiring. This autonomy was coupled with additional supports

including funding, an additional hour of schooling, and district-level instructional support staff.

In response, leaders were encouraged to adopt innovative strategies responsive to schools’

unique academic and cultural needs. However, in the years during this study, the district

experienced tectonic shifts in academic expectations with the district-wide adoption of a more

rigorous curricula, state assessment, and accountability demands that emphasize academic

growth and proficiency. As a result, leaders within the study were balancing the demands of

turnaround in addition to a more restrictive educational environment.

School leaders were not only contending with a chronically low-achieving school, but in

a particular school within a specific neighborhood of this southern city, each with its own

complex legacy. Most of the leaders interviewed for this study considered themselves insiders,

either as longtime residents, students, and educators of the city or neighborhood where their

school was situated. As is discussed below, all had some conceptualization of the specific

communities their schools were located in and described how its social and historical context

influenced their work. Each, in turn, was in the process of reconciling their understanding of the

salience and significance of community identity and the demands of school turnaround.

## Methods

This paper is based upon over 20 semi-structured interviews conducted with 10 (fourteen)

district and school leaders. Among these are 10 (ten) current or former district principals and

assistant principals and 4 (four) district-level administrators who worked closely as instructional

or leadership support staff. The leaders belonged to five case-study schools (three high schools

and two K-8 schools. The data represent preliminary findings from an ongoing three-year case


<!-- Page 7 -->


DRAFT – PLEASE DO NOT DUPLICATE / CIRCULATE

6

study. Each interview was audio recorded and transcribed by a professional team. The

researchers then coded the transcripts with a computer software program using a set of codes

derived from the overarching research questions. For this investigation, the researcher identified

relevant portions of the transcribed interviews using codes relevant to the topic area. Since the

topic of this paper was not the sole purpose of the overall project, this process was done to

narrow the scope of interviews relevant to the paper’s chosen topic of focus.

The researcher adopted the thematic analysis structure suggested by Nowell and

colleagues (2017). After the relevant interviews were identified, the researcher read through each

transcript once to familiarize herself with the text. In addition to reviewing the transcripts, the

researcher also reviewed the field notes and interview summary documents completed during

and after the individual researchers as additional contextual evidence and support. Throughout

the analysis process these documents were used to compare the individual researcher’s

interpretation of the data alongside those of her colleagues. The next step of analysis included

reviewing the documents a second time. During this process the researcher created high-level

codes based upon themes pulled from the culturally responsive leadership literature identified by

Khalifa and colleagues (2018). These codes were then applied to the transcripts. The excerpts

selected were logged in an Excel spreadsheet and categorized by topic area in addition to

participant ID, school ID, and leadership role. These passages were then reviewed a second time.

Although the high-level categories were produced from the theoretical framework, these sub-

categories were developed directly from the data collected. The passages were then re-coded

using this more detailed coding schema. This was conducted by hand, where the researcher

created hard copies of the excel documents and coded lines of text. From this coded data, the

researcher composed a thematic matrix for a category-based analysis, focusing on topics that

would eventually guide the final conclusions (Kuckartz, 2014). From this process, we were able

to combine the findings into more cohesive or holistic themes which are presented below. To

ensure the validity of these themes, participant language was used to develop the final categories

(Nowell et al., 2017).

Findings

iZone leaders do not completely fulfill the core components of culturally responsive

practice. However, they do possess a shared acknowledgement of the value and the significance

of local history to the work of schooling. Leaders were also fiercely committed to serving these

communities by providing a quality educational experience. However, this dedication and

respect for community history and culture at times conflicted with the aims of school turnaround.

The analysis revealed that many leaders were actively negotiating how they could

simultaneously maintain and support community norms while pursuing the radical change

required of school turnaround.

Community Knowledge

Central to culturally responsive pedagogy is an understanding of the norms, practices,

and beliefs of a specific community and integrating these into the work of instruction. A variety

of scenarios required leaders to act as competent members of school communities, capable of

operating within cultural norms without sacrificing the high expectations and demands of school

turnaround. Leaders were not only aware of the significance of these histories but able to connect

it with the school’s culture and their ultimate vision for the school. Some benefited from deep

roots in the communities in which they served. An elementary school principal described how he

had grown up right around the corner from the school where he taught school.


<!-- Page 9 -->


DRAFT – PLEASE DO NOT DUPLICATE / CIRCULATE

8

I live in the zip code and my mom lives in this zip code. My church is in this zip code. This work is a bit more personal when you can do work that is at your doorstep. You feel like you are making a greater impact when you are touching the community that you live in.

Not only did this leader come from the neighborhood he serves in but retains ties to that

community beyond the professional. Here, he specifically connects that connection with a

special loyalty to his practice and his students. He even associates this connection with more

significant outcomes. Similarly, a high school principal noted that although he grew up in a

different city, he still feels a connection to his students due to their shared backgrounds of low-

income, black students. For him, this connection enables him to connect with students and

families on a personal level. While these interpretations may be a subjective perspective, it

illuminates how deeply personal connection to a space and community is engrained in his

leadership practice and metrics of success.

Whether transplants or homegrown, leaders provided detailed descriptions of

neighborhood character and identity that often drew upon historical narratives. For example, a

high school principal shared,

It’s a very historic neighborhood. There’s a lot of pride in the history of it being one of the first neighborhoods where African-Americans owned their own home. That tradition kind of continued through the 1900s […] But more recently, there has been more issues in the neighborhood, poverty, and crime, and just things that really affect our school.

Here, the leader is acknowledging the school community’s positive historical legacy which still

instills a sense of pride in older generations, despite its gradual decline into poverty. He is

wrestling with an acknowledgement of an uplifting historical narrative alongside contemporary

conditions that negatively impact schooling. He walks the line of what might be considered a

deficit perspective, naming harmful conditions while resisting defining communities entirely in


<!-- Page 10 -->


DRAFT – PLEASE DO NOT DUPLICATE / CIRCULATE

9

these terms. A leader at a K-8 school described a “duality” where school staff “hear about the

good” in a neighborhood but also “hear stories about this, how violence and different things

affect the lives of your students.” Again, this comment, and others like it, exemplify how school

leaders resisted simplistic descriptions of school neighborhoods. Instead, leaders attempted to

acknowledge and find value in community culture and identity. These comments echo the voice

of a turnaround leader, who is aware of the negative quality and conditions of instruction that

necessitate turnaround work. At the same time, leaders attempt to uplift and find value in

neighborhood identity, viewing these as assets to schools and students.

Alumni organizations and other established community groups challenged leaders’

abilities to respect cultural norms while pursuing radical academic progress. Several of the

schools came with a highly engaged alumni population. A principal with a particularly engaged

alumni network remarked that, “all of their [the school’s] alum are just so proud that they went

here. So that also encouraged me to come check out.” For this principal, having a legacy of pride

and excitement was a selling point for working in the school, despite its many challenges.

Another principal remarked that alumni engagement in his interviewing process was also an

encouragement. They were inspired by the passion alumni had for their schools. While a

dedicated alumni network can and did serve as an asset to the work of school leaders, school

leaders had to invest energy in creating and maintaining a positive relationship. The give and

take of negotiations with alumni and other engaged school actors at times functioned as a point

of tension. Turnaround work often comes at the price of rapid change which challenged the

established norms in some communities. Leaders proved attune to these points of convergence

and divergence taking opportunities to collaborate when possible. One leader described a “kind

of disconnect […] between the alumni of [the school] who live in the neighborhood, and support

the neighborhood, and love the neighborhood, and them seeing what’s happening at the school

today.” In conversations with engaged alumni, this principal made sure to acknowledge the

positivity, like a highly successful basketball team. He also connected new educational initiatives

to reclaim past educational success. Adopting such policies indicates an embrace of culturally

responsive tactics, in a clear integration of community perspectives into the work of school

turnaround. Sometimes, they could successfully balance the academic transformation of

turnaround with community expectations. However, it was unclear if this was always a

successful negotiation. However, those leaders with highly involved alumni did not mention

conflict between them.

Passion for Turnaround Work

Leaders shared a personal passion for school turnaround fueled by professional experiences or

personal connections to the work. In many instances, leaders interviewed cut their teeth in

turnaround schools either as teachers or principals. Many underwent extensive training to

prepare for the role participating in national programs such as the New Leaders program. Others

described specifically pursuing the challenge of turnaround work. During one principal’s

interview he requested to be in the school that had the highest possible need. He wanted to “take

those same skill sets and put them in place where they say it can’t be done.” After already

experiencing success in a previous school, he welcomed the challenge of a chronically “failing”

context. Another principal who previously worked in a more affluent part of Memphis said he

wanted to work with low-income communities of color. He shared that he looked for positions

where

the odds aren’t most attractive because of the challenge of the work. Doing turnaround work as well as working with specifically minority students. I came from more diverse

11

background in the suburbs. And I specifically wanted to work in urban impoverish with minorities. The challenge of the work, going where no one else was willing to go, was core to their selection

of position. Also within this is a connection to some tenets of culturally responsive leadership.

Specifically, a desire to serve communities of color.

School leaders felt responsibility for spreading this passion to their colleagues. Many

were invested in building a coalition of actors within and beyond the school with a unified vision

of school turnaround. For many it began in the school. Teachers and administrators needed to

share a commitment to the work of turnaround, including the challenge of the work. Leaders

perceive themselves as responsible for igniting a collective passion and commitment to their

work. For instance, a high school principal described his philosophy,

And we asked them [the school staff] what are we going to do? Because that’s my leadership style. Of course, I have a vision. But they have a stake in that vision and they’re the experts, and I hired them to do a job and I need [their] input on what we’re going to do. So we talked about it and we said, “You’re all going to do exactly what we did the year before. We’re going to take them and we’re going to roll up our sleeves and we’re going to get to work.” So we did.

Principals and other leaders shared similar perspectives. As in this instance, leaders described

repeatedly messaging these beliefs to their staff. Leaders were engaged in building a turnaround

community embedded within and dedicated to serving the broader one. While creating a unified

vision is also present in culturally responsive leadership literature, the principals interviewed did

not make explicit connections to such practices. An exception can be found in how leaders

conceptualized success.

Leaders expressed sometimes contradictory ideas of what success in a turnaround context

meant. The most prevalent theme in leader “visions” of gains and high performance was “point

gains” on achievement tests or moving from one district achievement level to another. These

12

perspectives carry with them a common theme in turnaround work, where success is measured

by standardized test performance. An exception to this might be found in the high expectations

on student performance. Beyond this, some leaders pushed against normative turnaround

perspectives of achievement. One acknowledged that, “even though we’re still a little bit below

where we need to be, hopefully by the end of this school year they will be proud of what they did

and proud of what they learned. That’s my goal. That’s what’s most promising for me.” Here,

having students feel “proud” of their progress supersedes desires for meeting performance

targets. Similarly, the same principal who boasted about “double digit gains” in standardized test

scores, also said that he prioritized helping students “see beyond these four walls,” or imaging

better lives for themselves. While the latter goal is not mutually exclusive with the former, it

does elevate goals for students that are more reminiscent of culturally responsive than turnaround

values. His comments border on a critical consciousness, where students realization of their

personal spiritual or emotional growth is emphasized over normative constructions of academic

success.

## Conclusion

Leader commentary, like this paper, show an idea on the edge of realization. It applies two

perspectives—critically responsive leadership (CRL) and turnaround leadership—and considers

where such practices might exist alongside each other. Specifically, it explores the experiences

and testimonies of Transform School leaders to see where these frameworks take shape within

practice. There is no perfect alignment. Just as leaders begin showing a commitment to the

principles of CRL, they reassert a commitment to turnaround practices. This is not to say that the

two cannot exist alongside or support each other. On the contrary, this is a preliminary


<!-- Page 14 -->


DRAFT – PLEASE DO NOT DUPLICATE / CIRCULATE

13

exploration into the points of resonance between the two. As an exploratory study, this paper is a

jumping off point for thinking more deeply and critically about where these two points converge.

A potential next step would be to investigate district and school leaders intentionally

constructing culturally responsive identities within a turnaround context.
